A.explanation: At an ammeter reading of $0.2\text{ A}$ the curve shows a true current of only about $0.1\text{ A}$, so the error is large.

B.explanation: At an ammeter reading of $0.4\text{ A}$ the true current is only about $0.25\text{ A}$, so the ammeter still reads much too high.

C.explanation: At an ammeter reading of $0.6\text{ A}$ the true current is about $0.4\text{ A}$, so a clear positive systematic error remains.

D.explanation: At an ammeter reading of $0.8\text{ A}$ the curve is closest to the line where reading equals true current, with true current about $0.75\text{ A}$.

hints: Look at the axes of the calibration graph: the vertical axis is ammeter reading / $\text{A}$ and the horizontal axis is true current / $\text{A}$.
Nearest to the true current means the point on the curved calibration line with the smallest vertical gap from the line where ammeter reading equals true current.
For each listed reading, go across from the vertical axis to the curve and then down to the true-current axis, and judge which vertical gap is smallest near $1.0\text{ A}$.
walkthrough: Identify the axes: $y$ is the faulty ammeter reading in $\text{A}$ and $x$ is the true current in $\text{A}$ from $0$ to $1.0\text{ A}$.
The reading is most accurate where the calibration curve is closest to equal values, that is where $\text{ammeter reading} = \text{true current}$.

Read the curve: at low $x$ it rises steeply above the origin, so a $0.2\text{ A}$ reading corresponds to only about $0.1\text{ A}$ true current, and a $0.4\text{ A}$ reading corresponds to only about $0.25\text{ A}$.
Further along, a $0.6\text{ A}$ reading corresponds to about $0.4\text{ A}$ true current, still a difference of about $0.2\text{ A}$.
Near the top the curve flattens and meets the equal-value region: a $0.8\text{ A}$ reading corresponds to about $0.7$ to $0.8\text{ A}$ true current, a difference of only about $0.05\text{ A}$.
This smallest difference occurs at the highest listed reading. This is option D
